podcast.title: C.G.Jung Helpdesk
podcast.note: Episodes referenced by number/title in this draft; the app will key them to feed GUIDs automatically.

onboarding.prompt: What do you want to explore?

topics.name: The Map of the Psyche
topics.tagline: Jung's core model, from the ground up
topics.about: Jung's model of the mind, built from the ground up: how consciousness rises out of something far older, how complexes and associations shape what you perceive, and why the parts you neglect never stop working. By the end, the vocabulary the whole podcast speaks is yours: archetypes, complexes, the collective unconscious.

topics.name: Types & Functions
topics.tagline: Introverts, extraverts, and the function you never trained
topics.about: Jung's map of how people differ: the two attitudes, the four functions, and the inferior one that trips you up at exactly the wrong moment. Intuition and the irrational get their due, and logos and eros show how the differences play out between people. Useful the day after you hear it.

topics.name: Shadow, Self & Individuation
topics.tagline: The inner cast of characters and the path to wholeness
topics.about: The inner cast of characters: the shadow you'd rather not own, the persona you show the world, the other that speaks with your voice. This is the path Jung called individuation: the slow negotiation between everything you are, aimed at the Self that holds it together.

topics.name: Dreams, Symbols & the Numinous
topics.tagline: Where the unconscious speaks: dreams, alchemy, synchronicity
topics.about: Where the unconscious speaks in its own language: dreams, symbols, alchemy, synchronicity. The strange territory Jung refused to abandon to superstition. Expect the mystical taken seriously and examined carefully, from active imagination to tarot and UFOs.

topics.name: Jung at the Movies
topics.tagline: Film analyses through a Jungian lens
topics.about: Jung at the cinema: eight films read through his ideas, from the shadow burning through Fight Club to the persona with nothing behind it in American Psycho. The lightest door into the concepts: you already know these stories; now watch them confess their psychology.

topics.name: Jung in Everyday Life
topics.tagline: Relationships, family, body, nature, and the self-help question
topics.about: Jung off the page and in a life: family and childhood, relationships, the body, nature, suffering, and what therapy and self-help can honestly promise. Where the theory has to prove it can help an actual Tuesday.

topics.name: Jung Himself
topics.tagline: The man himself: his books, his quarrels, his patients
topics.about: Jung the man, not the model: which books to read and in what order, the break with Freud, the ways he is misread and the places where even his host disagrees with him, his view of East and West, and the patients whose stories carry his ideas. For when you want to know who was talking.

unassigned: Intro (trailer, plays from the About screen, not part of a journey)

links.why: The sun's arc, told as the history of consciousness
The centre the whole arc turns around
Life begins as a child's

takeaways: Jung draws a life like the sun's day: it rises out of the horizon, stands at noon, and goes down again.
A small child has almost no ego; consciousness surfaces slowly, like a little island coming out of the sea.
The first half of life is for getting out of your parents' basement and establishing yourself in the world.
Around 38 the old solutions stop working and the unconscious pushes you inward; today we call it the midlife crisis.
Consciousness lags behind the unconscious the way you hear a plane where it was, not where it is.

chapters.title: The Secret of the Golden Flower
Hearing the plane, not seeing it

links.why: The same ground, revisited seven years deeper
Where the primordial images become art

takeaways: Freud's unconscious is the cellar under your house; Jung says all the cellars are connected, and that is the collective unconscious.
An archetype is a primordial image and a pattern of behaviour, inborn the way a bird knows how to build a nest.
Every culture has a dragon and nobody ever saw one; coincidences like that across cultures pointed Jung to archetypes.
You never meet an archetype directly; you see what it structures, like a crystal forming out of water.
Archetypes bring fascination or fear and are stronger than you; culture and ritual are the safety nets for living them.

chapters.title: The books beyond the Collected Works
The dream of the deep cellar
Why you should not seek archetypes
The earache that was a tooth

links.why: From diagnosis to what therapy can do
The intruders behind the symptoms
The psychiatric years before Freud

takeaways: A complex is a gremlin in the mind: an emotion tied to associations, the buttons someone knows how to push.
Having complexes is normal, like cancer cells the immune system clears every day; a neurosis is the trash you never took out.
In Jaws the shark keeps coming closer until Brody turns and faces it; an ignored problem does the same.
The problem is in the present, not the childhood; blocked libido flows back, and the neurosis itself is a healing mechanism, like a fever.
Hysteria is a complex grown into a second personality; psychosis and schizophrenia are the collective unconscious breaking through and replacing reality.

chapters.title: Complexes, the gremlins in the mind
Brody and the shark in Jaws

links.why: Reading Jung without misreading him
The archetypes talk this one builds on

takeaways: Jung's writing comes in three blocks, the psychoanalytic years, the collective unconscious, then alchemy, and each one builds on the last.
Start with Memories, Dreams, Reflections; understanding his life makes the work easier to understand.
The collections of short talks and essays are easier than the big books, because Jung was a better talker than writer.
For any alchemy book, read the last chapter first; that is where he says what he was trying to get at.
If a Jung book has dream in the title, get it; the dream seminars are the best reading he left.

chapters.title: How the Collected Works are built
UFOs, Wotan and Answer to Job
Alchemy, read the last chapter first
Letters, talks and the dream seminars
The Red Book and two scams

links.why: Consciousness, examined on its own
From the history of consciousness to how it perceives

takeaways: Consciousness, for Jung, is the ability to discriminate: switch the light on and the dark room becomes a bed, a cupboard, a pillow.
Early humans lived in participation mystique: the Pueblo Indians believed their morning ritual made the sun rise.
The Greeks were not angry, Ares drove into them: emotions were met outside as gods before anyone owned them inside.
Taboos, politeness and laws were the first workouts for a fragile consciousness; a taboo trains you to watch yourself.
Psychology appeared only when religion stopped doing its job and people were left alone with their own psyche.

chapters.title: The sharp spot in the eye
From one life to all humanity
No need to count the sheep

links.why: Fantasy, the psyche's own energy at work
Libido, felt in the body

takeaways: Libido for Jung is not sex drive but psychic energy: neutral like the sun, it cannot get lost, only move somewhere else.
Consciousness is born out of the unconscious; hit your head, or crash the car, and you are suddenly fully awake.
The sea's surface is the threshold; sleep, stress, alcohol or meditation lower it, and in dreams the fish come up.
His dreams of a schoolgirl from years ago turned out to be a billboard he drove past every day without noticing.
Raising something from the unconscious takes energy: remembering, reflecting, looking at a church a little longer, or active imagination.

chapters.title: Hit your head to wake up
How things sink and get repressed
What rises up on its own

links.why: The function you neglect holds the treasure
The strangest of the four functions
The astrology evening he promised here

takeaways: Extraversion and introversion are Jung's own words: one orients to the objects outside, the other to the subject inside.
Four functions feed the ego: sensation says what is there, thinking what it is, feeling its value, intuition where it might go.
Your strongest function is the superior one; its opposite becomes the inferior function, as clumsy as brushing your teeth left-handed.
The inferior function is the fun part, Jung says, because the most potential sits in what you have always ignored.
People pick partners who cover their inferior side, the thinker a feeler, the businessman an artist; types are instruments, not boxes.

chapters.title: Eight years on one thick book
Four channels and a botched quote

links.why: The child's world, on its own terms
When the child refuses to grow up

takeaways: A neurotic small child is never the child's problem; unfiltered, it picks up what the parents have not dealt with, their unlived life.
Logos separates like a sword, Eros joins; the side foreign to you turns up as anima or animus, and in the partner you fall for.
Projection heaps what you will not admit about yourself onto the people closest to you, and the partner is the first victim.
In education what you do counts more than what you say; children react to who you are.
A mother complex makes the Don Juan who hunts the mother in every woman, or the good boy who never leaves the basement.

chapters.title: When a small child is neurotic
Why film lovers start out hating
Heaping your shadow on a partner

links.why: Active imagination is fantasy taken seriously
When active imagination becomes art

takeaways: Jung spent thirteen secret years on The Red Book; the alchemists turned out to be his control group, and a thirty-year obsession began.
They saw lions and dragons in their flames and acids; they were projecting their own psyche onto matter without knowing it.
Chemistry threw alchemy out as nonsense, but Jung says chemists were the wrong readers: the texts describe psychology, not materials.
The lapis, the incorruptible gold, is the Self: what you are, unified with everything you have not yet integrated.
Active imagination is confronting your fantasies on your own terms, holding one still and uncritically, exactly as the alchemists did.

chapters.title: The secret of The Red Book
The Golden Flower in the post

links.why: Aions, given their own evening
Where synchronicity meets physics

takeaways: Young Jung was a mythbuster: the medium moved the table herself, and the haunted room held traces his nose picked up.
Causality asks how the hat got onto the beach; synchronicity asks what it means that hat, kissing couple and birds are there now.
Astrology, for Jung, is the first psychology: people projected their psyche onto blinking lights and named them after gods.
The signs have drifted 4,000 years, so if birth time shapes personality, it is time inside the psyche, not the stars.
Aions are the collective unconscious ageing: when Pisces began, fish-centred Christians replaced achievement-mad Rome within two centuries.

chapters.title: I Ching sticks and tarot cards
The sky as a projection screen
Aion and Jesus as a fish

links.why: Associations, the raw material of dream-reading
Dreams, but by daylight
The mechanics behind it, told in Mother, Father, Child

takeaways: Kekulé dreamt the benzene ring, Watson the double helix, and a truck driver dreamt The Terminator; dreams are not random.
A dream is a natural product, like a deer in the forest: it does not care about you and it is not a facade.
Dreams compensate the conscious attitude, so Jung first learned the dreamer's life, then asked for a series of fifty to a hundred dreams.
A sewing machine in a dream is a sewing machine, not a substitute; you follow the image, you do not swap it.
Read a dream as if it is making fun of you: whatever you overvalue, it shows as small.

chapters.title: A dream is like a deer

links.why: If perception filters everything, what is real?
The types that do the filtering

takeaways: Consciousness is a problem solver like Mr. Meeseeks: it shows up for the task, tires fast, and nobody becomes conscious without hitting their head.
We see colours, not wavelengths; everything arrives pre-filtered, and only what can dock onto something already known gets through.
Real is what works: a vision that changes how someone acts is as real as walking into a tree, only from inside.
Inside and outside land in one pot of psychic images; the ancients mislabelled it as gods in rivers and scales in the sky.
Consciousness pulls single colours out of the brown soup, and individuation is getting every colour back out.

chapters.title: Attitude and the shark in Jaws

links.why: Creation danced instead of painted
Pop art with a psychology to confess

takeaways: Past the midpoint of life Jung let established patients paint, to watch something in them create without their planning it.
Creation comes out of the unconscious; people do not have ideas, ideas have people, as with Ramanujan and Tesla.
An artist is not just flooded like a psychotic; the artist translates ancient collective material into the zeitgeist, sugar around the pill.
Before a creative burst the energy recedes like water before a tsunami, which from inside looks like depression.
Nothing wholly new is required; Da Vinci painted the Last Supper and nobody asked why he had no original story.

chapters.title: Why art need not be new

links.why: The mandala, symbol of the Self
The opposites a symbol must bridge
The symbols he saved up since the dreams talk

takeaways: Jung sees opposites everywhere; like a battery's two poles, the tension between them is where things happen, and stories run on it.
Push one opposite far enough and it flips into the other; Jung calls that enantiodromia, and the word best comes from bad.
Opposites cannot meet directly; they need a third, the child of man and woman, the hero who belongs to both worlds, like Luke Skywalker.
A symbol is the third between consciousness and the unconscious: known pieces arranged strangely, a mermaid, or a horse called a tall pig.
Water is the unconscious, fire libido, light consciousness; the West kills its dragons, the East integrates them.

chapters.title: Pushed too far, into the opposite
Why a sign is no symbol

links.why: The Self, the goal of the whole path
The price of wholeness

takeaways: Individuation means becoming a whole, indivisible individual; the oak is already in the acorn, and it happens whether you join in or not.
The first half of life is field research with collective goals; in the second your superior function fails and you must use your other hand.
The first stop is the shadow, projected onto people you cannot stand; owning it is a moral effort, and cynicism beats not being home.
The path is a spiral, not a line: do the next necessary thing, follow interest and fear, and do it with real people.
Integration costs an ego death, the phoenix, or Jack shooting himself in Fight Club; afterwards you hold the conflict without being pulled under.

chapters.title: The oak tree in the seed
The first half as field research
When your best tool goes blunt

links.why: When possession turns malignant

takeaways: Consciousness runs on small batteries; the ego's libido is spare change next to what the unconscious has in the back.
Inflation begins when what you can see looks like all there is: Dunning-Kruger in a hall of mirrors, driving fast with dirty windshields.
An activated archetype puts your life on rails, as love does, as lizard people did for one man, as the creative spirit did for Nietzsche.
Anima possession makes men driven and moody; animus possession gives women opinions out of nowhere; both are a veil over the eyes.
It starts as fascination, feels like endless power, and burns you out; the way back is a modest doubt: why has this idea taken me?

chapters.title: Not lord in your own house
Ten smart people in a group

links.why: The other figures beside the shadow
The misunderstandings, cleared up

takeaways: The shadow is everything consciousness pushed aside: the shameful parts, but also good qualities you never noticed you had.
Nothing in the psyche gets lost; what you ignore gathers in the dark and grows stronger the longer you ignore it.
You see other people's shadow at once and your own almost never; ask close friends, or watch yourself drunk, ill or stressed.
Projection is normal perception: colors are not in the wavelengths, and the burglar in the night noise is in you.
What you hate points to your shadow; evil always lies just across the Rhine, and killing Vader only shows Luke his own face.

chapters.title: Projection and the colours we see
Hate and the town next door
The young man and the teacher

links.why: Where the mandala's eastern side gets its own evening
Mandala drawing as active imagination

takeaways: The Self is the whole psyche, conscious and unconscious together; the ego circles it like a planet around the sun.
It is a marked-off, personal part of the collective unconscious: the oak already inside the acorn, a future you.
Your interests are the Self calling consciousness to come and grow; even the situations you land in are assembled by it.
Mandala is Sanskrit for circle: the symmetrical four-part patterns that appear in dreams and drawings when life is most chaotic.
It need not be drawn; a mosh pit or the circling at Mecca is already a mandala, but consciousness still has to unpack it.

chapters.title: A quick map of the psyche
Circle pits and moving in circles
The cross as a Western mandala

links.why: A persona of doll-perfect surfaces
The projection of unconscious femininity

takeaways: Consciousness is the bird, the unconscious the snake; the unconscious keeps interfering with your plans, and consciousness keeps repressing what does not fit.
Barbieland is sterile: no water, no animals, no death, every day the best day, which no real human could stand for long.
Barbie's thoughts of death are her inferior Logos surfacing; flat feet on the ground are the body pulling her down to earth.
Ken gets intrusive feelings instead, and with no man to explain the real world he copies the shiny surface: possession and inflation.
The outcasts save Barbieland, as repressed things do, and Barbie ends like Pinocchio: for the first time she wants something.

chapters.title: The old lady on the bench

links.why: What the quarrel left misunderstood
Dreams: where the two parted ways
The complexes talk he points to
Which books to read after the quarrel

takeaways: Jung's association test found words that made patients stall and forget; Freud's unconscious was the first concept that explained the data.
They talked thirteen hours at their first meeting; it ended, as professors end friendships, with a book Freud did not want.
Freud reduced everything to sexuality and the incest complex; Jung made libido a neutral psychic energy and asked why a fairy, not a mother.
For Jung a neurosis is a task failed now, not a childhood wound; you catch tuberculosis today, not from a childhood contact.
Freud found the cellar under the house; Jung found the tunnels connecting all cellars, and we are all Freudians now anyway.

links.why: Where the East locates evil
When the gods leave, they return in the sky
The controversial Jung, continued

takeaways: Consciousness grows by narrowing its focus, in a child and in a culture; what it leaves out pushes back to be lived.
Christianity was put on top of pagan Europe rather than growing from it, so the West has to force itself to believe.
India has five thousand uninterrupted years of elaborating the psyche; the West has a fragmented two thousand, and no school for life after forty.
East and West are each other's shadow: causality against synchronicity, the dragon killed against the dragon befriended, the cross against the Buddha under his tree.
You cannot copy the other side's homework; Westerners doing yoga stay on the surface, and the West's own yoga was alchemy.

chapters.title: Yin and yang, or the dragon

links.why: The shadow, in theory
The persona Tyler burns down
The side note that came out of the East and West evening

takeaways: Jack is trapped in Logos: insurance job, planes, apartment in the sky; his libido sits in the unconscious, so he is depressed and sleepless.
He hates Marla because she plays his own fraud back at him; the penguin in his cave says she is the mate for life.
Tyler is Marla in male form, a sugar-coated anima: he burns the apartment, takes Jack below ground, makes him stay with pain.
You can only sacrifice what you truly have; when Jack pulls the trigger Tyler vanishes and Marla is the one left holding his hand.
Tyler is also a collective shadow; Project Mayhem spreads like Wotan did in Weimar Germany, an archetype gripping a whole society.

chapters.title: The penguin in the icy cave

links.why: Where even a devotee still struggles
The misreadings that became self-help
The test for what is really Jung's

takeaways: Jung wrote hard on purpose, for academics; the academics ignored him and ordinary people wrote him letters, so read Man and His Symbols first.
There is no diagram of Jung: he saw himself as a botanist describing what grows, so even UFOs and haunted rooms get a psychological reading.
He says unconscious, never subconscious, and it is not a wonderland to visit; it comes by itself, like weather or a wolf.
Extraversion is not sociability, feeling is not emotion, the shadow is not just evil, and archetypes are patterns of behavior, uncounted.
Individuation has no numbered stages, only the next step, and none of it is an ought; he described, he did not prescribe.

links.why: Secrets keep you from dissolving into the group

takeaways: Persona is the actor's mask with a mouthpiece, per sonare; it is the reduced version of you that the outside world deals with.
You need one, like the cashier or the polite 'I'm fine', and alone at home you drop it and sing to yourself.
The pitfall is hiding behind it, the LinkedIn profile or the title, until the inner life goes unattended and compensates.
A group is dumber than its members: watercolors mixed turn brown, a concert boils down to yay and boo, a crowd becomes a stampede.
People do not have ideas, ideas have people; you cannot preach to a group, only talk to the individual in it.

links.why: Leaving the bosom of the family

takeaways: Everyone has Eros and Logos, binding and separating, like two hands; the one you favor is conscious, the other waits in the unconscious.
Jack is Rose's animus, the inner image of the other sex; love at first sight is recognizing that image in someone.
Trapped and about to jump, Rose wants to become unconscious, like Sleeping Beauty; the animus appears at exactly that moment to wake her.
She takes on his traits, spitting, lying, riding like a man, and she has to save herself; nobody can do that step for you.
Once integrated, Jack sinks back into the water, the unconscious, like Tyler vanishing; the ship itself is conscious hubris afloat on the deep.

links.why: Meeting the patient in their own reality
Where therapy still looks like psychoanalysis

takeaways: Not medical advice: Jung's therapy is a hundred years old, and the aim was never superhumans but getting people back into normal life.
Libido that is not spent where life asks for it, the cow left unmilked, ends up in the unconscious as a complex or depression.
There is no illness that is not also a failed cure; the aim is steadfast patience in the face of suffering, not happiness.
The therapist sits in the foreground with opinions and admits not knowing; against shadow plus anima it is then two against two.
Let people talk until they hit a complex, then push there; drawing it out and asking friends about your shadow brings chaos into the open.

chapters.title: A psyche spread over the world

links.why: The fear of what surfaces into consciousness
The sea beneath the island

takeaways: Brody's flaw is avoidance: he warns instead of acting, fled New York to an island though he fears water, and needs a slap to wake.
Water is the unconscious and the island is consciousness; the shark is what Brody ignored, surfacing bigger and closer until it reaches his son.
Sharks eat everything, says Hooper, and so does a complex: discarded things gather in the dark, dead-eyed until libido feeds them.
Hooper brings knowledge, Quint brings the shadow, abrasive, shark-like and possessed; Brody copies Quint and learns the knots, the swearing, the shooting.
The hero kills the dragon alone, with Quint's fire, Hooper's air and the shark's water; earth, the missing fourth, is his wife on land.

links.why: The books he still argues with
Where simplified Jung starts to hurt

takeaways: Jung's work is incredibly coherent over sixty years, but his symbol readings rest on a fixed dataset of myths with no way to test them.
The bear meant the feminine because the myth said so first; that is the sharpshooter who paints the target after the shot.
He warns the unconscious is bad weather and then makes it sound incredibly cool; he preaches the body and prescribes only talking.
Logos, thinking, male, conscious on one side and Eros, feeling, female, unconscious on the other overlap so much they may be one thing.
One dream image can take him fifty pages, nobody else could repeat that, and his synchronicity leans on a misread of quantum physics.

links.why: Intuition, given cards to play with
Groups and their ground psychology, said there first

takeaways: Four ways information reaches you: sensation says there is something, thinking says what, feeling says whether you like it, intuition says what it could be.
Intuition is perception through the unconscious, Ahnung in German; Ramanujan got the solution first and worked out the proof afterwards.
Extraverted intuitives become hunters, gamblers, bankers and leaders; introverted ones become artists and prophets, and wisely keep quiet about it.
The intuitive sees the next peak through a telescope and feels already there; anything realized becomes a prison, and the stomach eventually sends the bill.
Down-to-earth sensation types get intuition as their inferior function, which is why they are the ones who see UFOs.

chapters.title: The modern mind thinks too much

links.why: Evil's home address: the shadow

takeaways: Evil is not the absence of good but its own force in the psyche; a tiger cannot be evil, only a human who can choose.
When instinct emerges, so does evil: what surfaces looks archaic first, and consciousness refines it, a river turned into a power plant.
A dream animal chasing you means you are at odds with an instinct; accept it and the explosion becomes a lion, then a cat.
Try hard to be wonderful and the shadow turns blacker, landing on a neighbor or a nation; we love villains because they carry it.
Christianity put body, earth, woman and devil in the same box below the Trinity; a God who is all-powerful cannot be only good.

links.why: The body, moving
The body's older home
Fear lives in the body first

takeaways: Jung explains the psyche through the body: you inherit a nose from one relative and a complex from another, and most of both runs unconsciously.
Body and soul are one thing; people who will not give something away get constipated, and a truth you cannot swallow shows in the throat.
The body pins you to one place and time, and that restriction is what makes consciousness possible at all; ears everywhere would hear nothing.
Libido has to manifest somewhere; the creative person who stops creating is the cow nobody milks, and secrets bottle it up the same way.
Christianity despised the body and the West is now rediscovering it, gyms, supplements, nude beaches; Jung noticed all this and still gave no bodily advice.

links.why: Children's dreams, continued
Ken, the puer in plastic
The eternal youth of self-improvement

takeaways: The puer aeternus, the eternal boy, is an archetype: adolescent energy, hopeful one-sidedness, life in blind sprouting forms.
Become too reasonable and adapted and the boy turns up in your dreams to compensate, so you do not dry up in your own adaptation.
What breaks the eternal boy is the anima: Simba leaves Timon and Pumbaa when Nala arrives, and the LAN party showers when girls show up.
Jung read Nazi Germany as a whole nation gripped by the puer, east of the Rhine where the wise old man was missing.
Beware of children in your dreams: a two-year-old points to something born in your psyche two years ago, like the patient's buried feeling.

links.why: The first Jungian idea of all
Where the podcast began: Jung's view of a life

takeaways: Jung splits everything into opposites, male and female, conscious and unconscious, because the tension between two poles is what makes anything move.
Whatever you label strongly, liked or disliked, carries value; the disagreeable side is where development runs, which is why not everybody is enlightened.
Alchemy interested him because turning lead into gold is a picture of the psyche: the value is already in the common thing.
Nothing is a coincidence for Jung: a fairy in your dream is there for a reason, and everything connects through patterns he calls archetypes.
He starts from the phenomenon and builds the theory after; Freud stopped at his model, Jung never stopped, which makes him hard to grasp.

chapters.title: The unconscious as a wrapped present

links.why: The experiment that revealed the complexes
The complex, seen in his patients

takeaways: A complex is a gremlin in the psyche, a split-off part with its own agenda, and Jung called his whole psychology complex psychology.
You notice complexes before anything else: slips of the tongue, accidents, forgetting mid-sentence, being in love, or rattling on for thirty minutes about one topic.
Complexes are normal, like gut bacteria; ignored, they grow in the dark like a cancer and drain the energy you feel missing as depression.
In the unconscious a complex stays frozen like a wound that never closed; it is only overcome when lived out to the full.
Jung found complexes with a stopwatch: in the association experiment, the words people answered slowly were the ones they could not repeat.

chapters.title: A shadow government of the ego
Drinking it down to the dregs

links.why: Spring outside, spring inside
Dreams of children, from the puer evening
Nature with teeth

takeaways: Go deep enough into the psyche and it becomes nature, and nature is autonomous and unconscious: it rains whether you want it or not.
Nature never preserves: consciousness is a net, and a diamond you do not recognize gets carried off by the river and ground to dust.
Consciousness is a deviation from nature, the Lucifer and Prometheus story, and we build ourselves a second nature of straight lines and right angles.
The unconscious is a compass needle, not a loving father; waiting for the right dream before you decide is the wrong idea.
Going to the woods makes you a little unconscious, a relief from the city, which is why the church lost missionaries to the Matterhorn.

links.why: The dreams talk he recommends mid-episode
Children and the natural mind

takeaways: A newborn has no ego or will, just impulses, but it is no blank slate; the personality is already there, dormant like handedness.
A child is the child of two families, not two parents, and the black sheep is often the one closest to the family spirit.
Children perceive what parents do, not what they say, and live out the unlived life of their parents.
So Jung says a child is never neurotic: the fever belongs to the parents, and when their problem is solved the child's symptoms disappear.
Fairy tales are not indoctrination; they give order to what already comes up in a child, like anger, as religion does for adults.

chapters.title: The unlived life of the parents

links.why: Associations shape what we perceive
The patients of the word-association tests

takeaways: The association experiment is early Jung, fresh from university, in a dry book full of tables that made him famous in America before Freud.
The setup is like sonar: a hundred stimulus words, say the first thing that comes to mind, and a Swiss watch timing every answer.
Run the list twice: quick answers repeat, slow ones do not, and the slow spots mark something hidden that he would later call a complex.
Adding skin conductivity made Jung the father of the lie detector; his side career as police investigator ended when he got the wrong man jailed.
A dream is the association experiment turned inside out: it supplies the stimulus words, and life itself is one big association experiment.

links.why: The first rule of Fight Club is a secret
A secret life in a tailored suit

takeaways: Jung calls secrecy a cancer in society, yet we love secrets in stories; Breaking Bad works because we know Walter White's must come out.
A repressed secret is not gone; it sits in the personal unconscious like an ignored animal in the apartment, and the trouble is neurosis.
The patient dreaming of a fiery wheel thought he was crazy until Jung handed him a 400-year-old alchemy book with the same picture.
Loneliness is not having no people around but being unable to say what matters; confession, drawing or a therapist gets the trapped libido moving again.
Secrets do have one use: having one to guard is a first, clumsy step toward individuation, which is why people invent secret societies.

links.why: Logos and Eros, the principles behind the figures

takeaways: The other is an alien will inside you with its own agenda; every figure in your dream is a split-off part of your psyche.
The unconscious shows up with a face because humans put faces on everything, from Teletubbies to deli meat to humanoid robots.
Shadow, anima and Self are not separate beings; like pulling yellow back out of brown watercolor, what is left looks different each time.
Your attitude decides how the other looks: for a shell-shocked soldier the bang became a lion, then a kitten you could play with.
Integration happens outside too: the neighbor you hate out of eight billion people is showing you your own shadow.

chapters.title: The soldier's lion becomes a cat

links.why: The aeons as the long history of consciousness
Archetypes on the scale of ages

takeaways: An Aion is roughly 2,000 years, one twelfth of the sun's own circle, and Jung says humanity develops in stages that match the zodiac signs.
The Egyptians had a battery and the Greeks a steam device, but nothing caught on; the seed was there, the ground was not ready.
Astrology is not stars influencing you; it is the collective psyche projected onto shiny lights in the night sky 3,500 years ago.
People wanted to talk about fish before Jesus arrived; Pisces has two fish, a vertical spiritual millennium and a horizontal material one.
Aquarius carries both fish in one vessel, its symbol the hermaphrodite; Jung wrote it decades before today's gender debate, a tough pill to swallow.

chapters.title: Why Jesus is like a fish

links.why: Real is what has an effect, fantasy included

takeaways: Real is what has an effect, Wirklichkeit ist was wirkt; it does not matter whether the thing is outside or inside you.
Jodie Foster in Contact was gone less than a second and nobody believed her; Jung took such experiences seriously, that is the whole talking cure.
You never meet reality directly; millions of impressions get filtered through your psyche, and changing the filter changes the world you live in.
Consciousness adapts like the immune system, many wiggly arms until one grips; it has to break and heal again every time something new arrives.
Plato wants you out of the cave into the sun; Jung says you only ever move to a nicer cave, and that is fine.

chapters.title: Real is what has an effect

links.why: The symbols evening this leans on

takeaways: Fantasies are waking dreams, and nothing man-made exists that did not start as one; the depth comes from the collective unconscious, not from consciousness.
When you have tried everything and are stuck, the leap of insight that arrives is the transcendent function: write drunk, edit sober.
Libido that hits an obstacle flows back into fantasy like a car with the handbrake on; the fantasy shows you what you are shirking.
Three ways to meet a fantasy: be overwhelmed, indulge it, or confront and materialize it; sometimes a good smack, Jung says, breaks the fascination.
Individuation is only ever the next logical step; clean the apartment and the next thing to fix appears, like Jacob's Ladder.

chapters.title: Shell shock, a lion, a kitten
The urge to make it permanent

links.why: A persona with nothing behind it
Possession, by instinct
Bateman's violence as fantasy

takeaways: Bateman's last line, this confession has meant nothing, is the point: no catharsis, and Jung says isolation is what drives people crazy.
He is all persona, the mask you speak through, and sensitiveness is a sure sign of inferiority: a better business card means murder.
Luis kissing his hand is the shadow offering love instead of hate, a first integration, and it freaks him out more than anything.
He is pure Logos, dissecting people and bodies while creating nothing; the cut-up women in his calendar point to a mother complex.
The movie mirrors a modern condition, all consciousness and no contact with the psyche, which is why Bateman memes and morning routines are everywhere.

links.why: Making things conscious as the Jungian mark
Waking up, as consciousness does

takeaways: The ego is the I at the center, and consciousness is everything connected to it, like a spider in its web; the rest is unconscious.
Jung never says subconscious; the unconscious is not below you, it is all around, and your future is in it as much as your past.
Consciousness separates, sorts and gives direction; it lets you willfully do things and willfully not do them, which a lion cannot.
No one gets conscious without suffering: consciousness switches on when the motor stops on the way to work, not while everything runs.
It is limited, one-sided and easily exhausted, a net with big holes; dreams are the partner who noticed what you missed all day.

links.why: Eros without Logos
The split-off parts we marry
From Rose to Maggie: two women choosing a self
Two films about a woman finding out who is doing the choosing

takeaways: Maggie likes her eggs however her fiancé likes them; Eros without Logos is blind relatedness, and the eggs Benedict scene is her finding herself.
Until you make the unconscious conscious it directs your life and you call it fate; she needs Ike, an outsider, to see her own pattern.
Ike is Logos, a writer in a penthouse with white hair; Maggie is Eros, brown-eyed on a farm; only different things can enter relationship.
Three failed weddings and a fourth that works differently is the alchemists' three-plus-one problem; four is wholeness, and the fourth is always the strange one.
Nobody individuates alone at home; it happens through other people, and the kiss followed by we need to talk is the grown-up part.

chapters.title: Logos, Eros and the round people
The problem of three plus one

links.why: Sacrifice's other face: rebirth
A sacrifice at the end of the voyage

takeaways: You only have emotions where you are not adapted; suffering is feedback, and hitting your head is the fastest way to become conscious.
Not all suffering is the same: behind a neurosis hides the natural suffering you were unwilling to bear, so it does not fix itself.
Sacrifice is a deliberate surrender, not being taken; it proves you have a self to give, like befriending the rabid dog in your apartment.
The hero needs a self-destructive streak; firefighters run in when everyone runs out, and the dragon gets fought because it stared long enough.
The crucifixion happens where you believe most in yourself: Jung's own intellect had to die, his vision of Siegfried, before the Red Book could come.

chapters.title: The dark night of the soul
Emotion where you are not adapted

links.why: The anima transforms everything it touches
The inflation of a king of the world
Evil with a Cuban accent

takeaways: Tony Montana is a man possessed by his anima, the feminine side that makes worldly things magical and sends him anywhere to get them.
The restaurant speech, is this it, is the midpoint shift; the first half of life expands outward, the afternoon must look within.
The hardest thing to stand is not suffering but success; it inflates the ego like a balloon, and down you come with a crash.
Elvira is empty achievement, Manny the contentment Tony cannot reach; killing Manny kills his last link to humanity, and you see it in his face.
We love villains because someone else carries our devil; Jung even names Al Capone, whose nickname was Scarface.

links.why: The acausal, by its older name
Fantasy, the irrational at work
Intuition, the irrational function

takeaways: After the break with Freud, a successful man near forty sat at the lakeshore building sandcastles because that is what occurred to him.
Sensation and intuition are the irrational functions, not unreasonable but empirical: a dream walks in like a deer in the woods.
A patient too set in her ways dreams of a scarab, a beetle taps the window, and the weirdness finally opens her up.
Smile at the talking squirrel but do not make a system of it, or the goblins disappear and you get ghosts instead.
A letter promises Freud he will return from astrology and the occult with rich booty; he never did, and the sandcastles became the Red Book.

links.why: What physics says about the perceiver
Reality, measured and imagined
Energy, the concept physics lent him
Pauli, physics and the alchemical process

takeaways: Einstein needed only paper, pencil and thought experiments to anticipate what Michelson and Morley spent millions failing to measure.
Jung's reading of quantum observation: look long enough into a dark hole and you perceive what is looking in.
An archetype is like gravity, never measured directly, only inferred from the many expressions it leaves behind.
Synchronicity, worked out with the physicist Pauli, names coincidences connected by meaning rather than cause, like three hurt arms in three days.
Odd numbers move and even numbers rest, which is why the play button is a triangle and stop is a square.

links.why: Rebirth as the shape of individuation
The age of Pisces and its Christ

takeaways: What dies goes into the dark of the unconscious, like a seed into the earth, and gathers strength to return.
Osiris, Dionysus and Christ tell one story of being torn apart and reassembled, which Jung reads as a pattern of the psyche.
You begin life scattered, and analysis is gathering your projected parts back into one functioning center.
Rebirth does not end conflict; individuation means standing in the turmoil without being swallowed by it.
One rebirth is never enough; you develop in a spiral, passing the same point again but never at the same height.

chapters.title: A recap of suffering and sacrifice

links.why: Where the patterns of relating begin
Logos and eros between two people
Relationships happen in bodies
A love story read as projection

takeaways: You cannot see the world without seeing yourself; what you notice in other people passes through your own psyche first.
Falling in love is projection: the anima or animus turns the other person into a screen for your missing half.
The neighbor or colleague you hate most is often carrying a piece of your shadow that you would rather not own.
The figures inside you are like a dog in the apartment; ignore it and you both have a bad time.
There is no individuation on top of Mount Everest; relationships are what force you to hold on to yourself.

links.why: Projection, writ across the sky
The flying saucer as a mandala
Modern myths, from saucers to the Matrix

takeaways: Jung's one book on UFOs spends five of 150 pages on whether they are real; the rest asks why people see them.
When the psyche is in chaos it sends round symbols of order, mandalas; a disconnected age sees them in the sky instead.
The religious instinct did not vanish with the trolls under bridges; it now looks upward for wiser visitors with better technology.
Medieval sky paintings show someone watching the thing; modern UFO pictures show only the object, the body removed.
The down-to-earth witness proves nothing to Jung; precisely such a rational person needs something overwhelming to pull him back toward the center.

chapters.title: A late book on flying saucers

links.why: Eros moves, logos talks
The inferior function, from the evening before

takeaways: Logos divides, judges and clarifies; Eros relates, gathers and interweaves; Jung means principles everyone carries, not men and women.
To read a symbol, forget H2O and start from the body: water is wet, deep and hides things, so it means the unconscious.
The holiday meal is the interplay: you cut and separate the ingredients, then everyone eats one dish and becomes one body.
The neglected side comes back raw: Runaway Bride dissolves into her partner, and men try to replace Eros with reason.
From the Red Book: if you go to thinking, take your heart with you; if you go to love, take your head.

links.why: Cards, stars and meaningful coincidence
Tarot on the therapist's table
Why the irrational is not nonsense

takeaways: Jung said almost nothing about tarot: one passage calling it a picture of the flow of the unconscious, like the I Ching.
Marcus draws one card each morning; by evening it describes the day surprisingly often, and his mother now does the same.
The card matters less than your reaction to it; that reaction is projection, and projection is how you learn about yourself.
The Major Arcana are archetypal situations; drawing the Lovers reminds you that your heartbreak is not the first in history.
The golden scarab tapping on Jung's window shows the openness a reading needs: synchronicity, meaning that arrives by timing, not cause.

chapters.title: Comic books and a daily card

links.why: What is real, if not its effect?
The evil the inner voice knows

takeaways: Trinity's line, you have to see it to believe it, matches Jung's I don't need to believe, I know: that is gnosis.
The Gnostics turned Genesis around: the serpent that brought consciousness was the savior, and the Matrix tells the same story.
Morpheus is the Self, the inner voice that calls Neo awake; he even wears the serpent's snakeskin coat.
Cypher wants back into the illusion, like Jung's patient who said, now you have dragged me into this filthy world.
Trinity meets Neo first because the anima comes before the Self, and her kiss is the last push into rebirth.

chapters.title: Reading the film as a dream

links.why: Doubt about one's own evil
A shadow that takes over completely

takeaways: Two familiar definitions of shadow: the Mr. Hyde dark side, and everything the ego is not, like the hippie to the soldier.
Each figure from the unconscious carries the whole behind it; catch your fish without pulling up the entire lake.
People who live in the shadow, like Ross from Friends, are decent folk who put the wrong foot forward and doubt themselves.
Gaston has no shadow at all: white as milk, never wrong, and for that reason possessed by what he cannot see.
A shadow makes a flat letter look three-dimensional; a person with a visible shadow is complete, not perfect.

chapters.title: Drawing the map of the psyche
Gaston and no doubt at all

links.why: Movement as a symbol in the making
The circle dance and the mandala

takeaways: Circle pits, techno raves and Fight Club answer the same need: a culture living in its head rediscovers the body.
A ritual only works when you do it fully conscious; you can eat bread half asleep, but you cannot take communion in a dream.
Dancers whip themselves into the hunting mood before the hunt; we do the same when we circle a goal to charge it with energy.
Analysis is circumambulation: you walk around a problem or a dream from all sides until the meaning in the middle comes out.
The soul's natural movement is not a straight line; you circle the Self, and your actions slowly bring it forth.

links.why: Self-help's serious name: individuation
Enduring the inevitable suffering
A month after dancing and movement, the follow-up

takeaways: The one-line version of 57 books: life is about experiencing yourself.
Marcus fixed three things in his apartment and suddenly saw twenty more; what you have integrated changes what you can perceive.
Do the next most necessary thing with conviction, like the Hermit who sees no further than his own lamp.
Break what comes up into Jung's four functions: what is present, what it is, how you relate to it, where it leads.
Give it form: patients who wrote down their plans healed faster, and Jung built sandcastles when his career fell apart.

chapters.title: Not master in your own house

links.why: The danger in every archetype's appearance
The puer, an archetype at work
The archetype of an age

takeaways: Jung uses archetype three ways: a recurring image like the hero, a pattern like falling in love, a situation like the king's death.
An archetype needs both image and emotion; protesters in Indonesia and Nepal raise the One Piece flag because it stirs something.
When you reach the end of your wits the archetype steps in, like Tom Hanks making fire in Cast Away or landing on the Hudson.
Nobody has seen an archetype, and nobody had seen an atom either; both are known by their effects.
Inflation means the archetype rides you; Tristan and Isolde starving in the woods is romantic to read and madness to live.

chapters.title: Image, emotion and a pirate flag

links.why: The inferior function is where the shadow lives
The attitude types behind the functions

takeaways: You have four ways of taking in the world, sensation, thinking, feeling and intuition, and one favorite hand among them.
The opposite of your favorite is the inferior function: childlike, obsessive, and strong enough to walk you on a leash like the Devil card.
Pauli drank and fought in bars, Marx had no money and bad hygiene: the neglected side runs loose in brilliant people too.
You cannot go straight at the inferior function; a thinker reaches feeling by way of the body or intuition first.
Leave everything in the superior function and it sucks you dry; go where you are most afraid, that is where life is.

chapters.title: The inferior side of each type
Why the inferior function is life
The rejected stone and the fourth

links.why: Where the obsession with alchemy began
The opus as individuation
The cognitive functions, explained in depth there

takeaways: Alchemy is projected psychology: staring into the vapors, the alchemists saw not the miracle in the metal but the one inside themselves.
The gold is already in the lead; coal and diamond are the same carbon, rearranged into a higher order.
Four stages run black, white, red, yellow, the podcast's logo colors; the nigredo is the depression where the work begins.
The albedo is pure but sterile; the rubedo adds blood, bringing the separated opposites back together, which Jung calls the coniunctio.
The stone is found on the road and the dung heap: what you end with was there at the start, before you could see it.

chapters.title: From The Red Book to alchemy

links.why: What the patients kept secret
Where the therapy behind these stories is explained
The episode he recommends to go on with
The diagnoses behind the patient stories

takeaways: A girl who no longer heard her footsteps had never seen her body; Jung sent her home to look in the mirror.
The officer's heartache and lump in the throat were swallowed tears for a girl he claimed did not matter.
The golden scarab beetle at the window broke a rationalist patient's resistance; the therapy ran smoothly after that.
A patient on her way to drown herself bought a pair of shoes and was cured for three weeks; Jung told her to buy another.
Two patients each claimed to be Jesus; Jung put them in one room, and each saw at once that the other was mad.

chapters.title: Hypnosis and a pair of shoes

links.why: The personality evening this one deepens
Numbers and types: two of Jung's ways to sort what is really continuous
Introvert and extravert perceive the same room differently

takeaways: Jung coined the terms and insists on extraversion; extroversion, he said, is bad Latin.
Introversion and extraversion are not about sociability; they say which world you turn to first, the one within or the one without.
The extravert acts because the outside world seems dead without him; the introvert holds back because it seems far too alive.
Two youths at a castle: the introvert thrills at old manuscripts while the extravert yawns, and each goes home annoyed.
Neither attitude is wrong; the other side is still there, and ignored it bites from behind as obsessions or tactless judgments.
